title: Vaccines, Germs and Clean Surgery
bigQuestion: How did careful observation and testing show that tiny living germs cause many diseases?

story.title: The Pump on Broad Street
story.kicker: A London doctor follows the deaths street by street and finds the water pump at the center.
paragraphs: Late in the summer of 1854, cholera struck the Soho neighborhood of London. Within a few days, hundreds of people were sick. Cholera caused terrible diarrhea, and many people died within a day. Families fled. Shops closed. Most doctors blamed a bad smell in the air, which they called miasma.

Dr. John Snow did not agree. He had studied cholera in earlier outbreaks. He thought something in the drinking water carried the illness. So he walked the streets, knocked on doors and wrote down where each person who died had lived and where they got their water.

The pattern was clear. The deaths clustered around one public pump on Broad Street. Some people far away had died too, but many of them had walked to that pump because they liked its water. Workers at a nearby brewery, who drank beer made on site, mostly stayed well.

Snow showed his evidence to the local leaders. On September 8, 1854, they agreed to remove the handle from the pump, so no one could use it. The outbreak was already slowing by then, and Snow said so himself. But his map and his careful counting changed how people study disease. Today he is often called a father of epidemiology.
story.think: Snow did not see a germ. What kind of evidence did he use instead, and why was it convincing?

lessons.title: Jenner and Cowpox
lessons.mainIdea: In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that cowpox could protect a person from smallpox, the idea behind the first vaccine.
reading: In the 1700s, smallpox killed many people in every part of the world. Those who lived often had deep scars. In the English countryside, people noticed something strange. Milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease from cows, seemed not to catch smallpox.

Edward Jenner was a country doctor who took this story seriously. In 1796 he took material from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes. He put it into small cuts on the arm of a boy named James Phipps. Later he exposed the boy to smallpox. The boy did not get sick. Tests like this on a child would not be allowed today.

Jenner called his method *vaccination*, from the Latin word vacca, meaning cow. A *vaccine* trains the body to fight a disease before a real attack comes. Over the next two centuries, vaccination spread worldwide. In 1980 the World Health Organization declared smallpox gone from the earth.

words.d: a medicine that trains the body's defenses to fight a disease before it attacks
giving a vaccine; Jenner's word, from the Latin vacca, meaning cow
a deadly disease that caused fever and blisters; declared gone from the world in 1980

look.title: Jenner Reports His Work
look.text: Jenner described how people who had caught cowpox from cows seemed protected afterward from smallpox, and he reported the cases he had tested, including the boy James Phipps.
look.cite: Edward Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, 1798
look.prompt: Jenner started from something farm people had noticed. Why was it important that he then tested the idea?

check.q: What did milkmaids who had caught cowpox seem to avoid?
check.why: People noticed that milkmaids who had cowpox did not seem to catch smallpox, and Jenner tested that idea.

check.q: Where does the word vaccine come from?
choices: The name of a London street
check.why: Vaccine comes from the Latin vacca, meaning cow, because Jenner used cowpox.

check.q: When did the World Health Organization declare smallpox gone?
check.why: In 1980 the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated.

lessons.title: Semmelweis and Clean Hands
lessons.mainIdea: In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis showed that doctors washing their hands saved the lives of new mothers.
reading: In the 1840s, the Vienna General Hospital in Austria had two clinics where babies were born. In one, doctors and medical students helped mothers. In the other, midwives did. Many more mothers died of a fever after birth in the doctors' clinic. Families knew it and begged not to go there.

Dr. Ignaz Semmelweis wanted to know why. He noticed that doctors often came straight from studying the bodies of people who had died. Then a fellow doctor cut his finger during such a study and died of an illness like the mothers' fever. Semmelweis guessed that the doctors' hands carried something deadly.

In 1847 he made doctors wash their hands in a chlorine solution before seeing mothers. Deaths in his clinic fell sharply. Yet many doctors refused to believe him, and he could not explain what the harmful matter was. Today *hand hygiene* is one of the most important ways to stop *infection* in any hospital.

words.d: an illness caused when germs get into the body and grow
cleaning hands with soap and water or hand rub to remove germs

look.title: Two Clinics, One Difference
look.text: Picture two rooms in the same hospital. The same kind of mothers arrive in both. In one room, the helpers come in from studying the dead. In the other room, they do not. Far more mothers die in the first room.
look.prompt: What one difference did Semmelweis focus on? How did changing only that one thing make his test fair?

check.q: What did Semmelweis ask doctors to do in 1847?
choices: Wash their hands in a chlorine solution
Open the windows to let out bad air
check.why: Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorine solution before seeing mothers.

check.q: Why did more mothers die in the doctors' clinic?
choices: Doctors carried harmful matter on their hands from studying the dead
The midwives' clinic had better food
Mothers in that clinic were older
check.why: Semmelweis noticed doctors came from studying bodies and guessed their hands carried something deadly.

check.q: Why did many doctors at first reject his idea?
choices: He could not explain what the harmful matter was
He had no clinic of his own
He worked in London, not Vienna
check.why: Semmelweis's results were strong, but he could not yet explain the cause, and many doctors refused to believe him.

lessons.title: Surgery Without Pain
lessons.mainIdea: In 1846 a public operation in Boston showed that ether could put a patient to sleep so surgery caused no pain.
reading: Before the 1840s, surgery was a terrible ordeal. Patients were awake. Strong helpers held them down. Surgeons worked as fast as they could, sometimes in a minute or two, because the pain was so great. Many people chose to suffer with an illness rather than face the knife.

On October 16, 1846, at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, a dentist named William Morton gave a patient ether vapor to breathe. The patient fell into a deep sleep. The surgeon removed a growth from his neck. When the patient woke, he said he had felt no real pain. The room where it happened is now called the Ether Dome.

This was a public demonstration of *anesthesia*, a way to block pain during treatment. News spread quickly to Europe. Soon chloroform was used too. Anesthesia let surgeons work slowly and carefully. Today a doctor called an *anesthesiologist* watches the patient's breathing and heart the whole time.

words.d: medicine that blocks pain, often by putting a patient into a sleep-like state, during treatment
a doctor who gives anesthesia and watches the patient during surgery

look.title: A Slow, Careful Surgeon
look.text: Imagine two surgeons. One must finish in two minutes while the patient screams. The other can take an hour, check each step and stop to think, because the patient is asleep.
look.prompt: Which surgeon can do more delicate work? Explain how anesthesia changed what surgery could do.

check.q: Where was ether publicly shown to prevent pain in surgery in 1846?
check.why: The 1846 ether demonstration took place at Massachusetts General Hospital, in the room now called the Ether Dome.

check.q: Why did surgeons before anesthesia work very fast?
choices: Patients were awake and in great pain
Germs had not yet been discovered
Light was too dim to see
check.why: Without anesthesia patients felt everything, so surgeons worked as fast as they could.

check.q: What does an anesthesiologist do?
choices: Gives anesthesia and watches the patient during surgery
check.why: An anesthesiologist is the doctor who gives anesthesia and watches breathing and heart during surgery.

lessons.title: Snow's Map
lessons.mainIdea: John Snow mapped cholera deaths in 1854 and traced them to one water pump on Broad Street.
reading: In 1854 most people believed cholera spread through miasma, a bad smell rising from filth. John Snow thought cholera spread through dirty water. When cholera hit Soho, London, he had a chance to test his idea.

Snow marked each death on a street map. The marks crowded around the Broad Street pump. He also looked for cases that did not fit. A woman who lived far away had died, but she had the water brought from Broad Street because she liked its taste. Brewery workers nearby drank beer and mostly stayed well. These odd cases made his case stronger, not weaker.

Snow also compared two water companies in another part of London. Homes served by a company that drew water from a dirtier part of the River Thames had far more cholera deaths. The water, not the smell, was the link. Years later, other scientists found the cholera germ itself.

words.d: an illness spread through dirty water that causes severe diarrhea and loss of body water
the old idea that disease came from bad-smelling air

look.title: Snow Explains His Case
look.text: Snow wrote that nearly all the deaths had taken place a short distance from the Broad Street pump, and that the people who died far away could often be traced to drinking its water.
look.cite: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd edition, 1855
look.prompt: Why did Snow pay close attention to the deaths that happened far from the pump?

check.q: What did most people in 1854 believe caused cholera?
check.why: Most people then blamed miasma, a bad smell in the air; Snow challenged that idea.

check.q: Why did the brewery workers support Snow's idea?
choices: They drank beer made on site and mostly stayed well
They lived far from Broad Street
They all drank from the pump and died
They smelled the bad air every day
check.why: The brewery workers were near the pump but drank beer instead of pump water, and most stayed well.

check.q: What did Snow's study of two water companies show?
choices: Homes with dirtier river water had more cholera deaths
Both companies had the same number of deaths
Smell was worse near the cleaner company
check.why: Homes supplied with water from a dirtier part of the Thames had far more cholera deaths.

lessons.title: The Birth of Epidemiology
lessons.mainIdea: Epidemiology studies who gets sick, where and when, to find causes and stop disease from spreading.
reading: Snow never saw the cholera germ through a microscope. He found the cause by counting cases and looking for patterns in people, places and time. This kind of work is called *epidemiology*. An *epidemic* is an outbreak of disease that spreads to many people in an area at once.

Epidemiologists ask simple questions. Who got sick? Where did they live, work and eat? When did they get sick? What did the sick people share that the healthy people did not? The answers can point to a cause, like a pump, a food or a kind of contact.

Today disease detectives still work this way. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention trains people to track outbreaks, such as food poisoning from one restaurant. Like Snow, they draw maps, compare groups and share what they find so leaders can act.

words.d: the study of who gets sick, where and when, in order to find causes and prevent disease
an outbreak of disease that spreads to many people in one area at the same time
a sudden rise in cases of a disease in one place

look.title: The School Lunch Mystery
look.text: Twelve students feel sick on Tuesday afternoon. All twelve ate the chicken salad at lunch. Of the students who ate pizza instead, none felt sick. Students came from different classes and different buses.
look.prompt: Think like an epidemiologist. What do the sick students share? What would you check next?

check.q: What is epidemiology?
choices: The study of who gets sick, where and when
check.why: Epidemiology studies patterns of illness in people, places and time to find causes.

check.q: How did Snow find the cause of the Soho outbreak without seeing a germ?
choices: By counting cases and finding a pattern
By growing germs in a dish
check.why: Snow counted and mapped cases to find a pattern that pointed to the pump.

check.q: Which U.S. agency trains people to track outbreaks today?
choices: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
check.why: The CDC trains disease detectives who track outbreaks in the United States.

lessons.title: Pasteur and Pasteurization
lessons.mainIdea: Louis Pasteur showed that tiny living microbes cause spoiling and disease, and that gentle heating can kill them.
reading: In France in the 1850s and 1860s, wine and beer makers had a problem. Their drinks often went sour. They asked the chemist Louis Pasteur for help. Under a microscope he saw tiny living things, called *microbes*, growing in the spoiled drinks.

Pasteur found that heating the liquid gently, without boiling it, killed many of the harmful microbes. This is *pasteurization*, named after him. Later it was used for milk. Pasteurized milk has prevented a great deal of illness, especially in children.

Many people then believed that life could appear on its own from rotting matter. Pasteur tested this with flasks that had long curved necks. Dust and microbes from the air got stuck in the curve. The broth inside stayed clear. When he broke the neck, microbes got in and the broth spoiled. Microbes came from other microbes. This helped build *germ theory*: the idea that germs cause many diseases.

words.d: living things too small to see without a microscope, such as bacteria
heating a liquid gently to kill harmful microbes; named after Louis Pasteur
the idea, proved in the 1800s, that tiny germs cause many diseases

look.title: The Swan-Neck Flask
look.text: Two flasks hold the same boiled broth. One has a long, curved neck open to the air. The other has its neck broken off. Days later, the broken one is cloudy. The curved one is still clear.
look.prompt: Both flasks touch air. What is the one difference, and what does it tell you about where microbes come from?

check.q: What does pasteurization do?
choices: Gently heats a liquid to kill harmful microbes
check.why: Pasteurization gently heats a liquid, without boiling, to kill many harmful microbes.

check.q: Why did the broth in the curved-neck flask stay clear?
choices: Dust and microbes got trapped in the curve
It had no air at all
check.why: The curve trapped dust and microbes from the air, so none reached the broth.

check.q: What is germ theory?
choices: The idea that tiny germs cause many diseases
The idea that bad smells cause disease
The idea that life appears from rotting matter
The idea that cows cause smallpox
check.why: Germ theory says tiny living germs cause many diseases.

lessons.title: Pasteur and Rabies
lessons.mainIdea: In 1885 Pasteur's team gave a rabies vaccine to a bitten boy, Joseph Meister, who survived.
reading: Rabies is a disease spread by the bite of an infected animal, such as a dog, bat or raccoon. Once signs of rabies appear, it is almost always deadly. In the 1800s, people feared mad dogs for good reason.

Pasteur's team made a weakened form of the rabies germ from the spinal cords of infected rabbits, dried for different lengths of time. In July 1885, a mother brought her nine-year-old son, Joseph Meister, to Paris. A rabid dog had bitten him many times. The team gave him a series of shots over about ten days. He never developed rabies.

Rabies moves slowly from a bite toward the brain. That gives a vaccine time to work after the bite. This is still true today. If a person is bitten by an animal that might have rabies, doctors give shots right away. Anyone bitten by an animal should tell a trusted adult and see a doctor.

words.d: a disease spread by animal bites that attacks the brain; shots right after a bite prevent it
a germ made less harmful so it can train the body's defenses without causing illness

look.title: Chance and the Prepared Mind
look.text: Pasteur told listeners that in science, lucky chances help only those whose minds are already prepared to notice them.
look.cite: Louis Pasteur, lecture at the University of Lille, 1854
look.prompt: How do Jenner and Snow show this idea at work? Give one example.

check.q: Who was Joseph Meister?
choices: A boy bitten by a rabid dog who received Pasteur's vaccine in 1885
The surgeon at the Ether Dome
A brewery worker on Broad Street
check.why: Joseph Meister, age nine, was the bitten boy who received Pasteur's rabies vaccine and survived.

check.q: Why can a rabies vaccine work even after a bite?
choices: Rabies moves slowly from the bite toward the brain
check.why: Rabies travels slowly toward the brain, which gives the vaccine time to work.

check.q: What should a person do after being bitten by an animal that might have rabies?
choices: Tell a trusted adult and see a doctor right away
Wait to see if signs appear
Wash it and forget about it
check.why: Doctors give rabies shots right after a possible exposure, so seeing a doctor quickly matters.

lessons.title: Koch Finds the Germs
lessons.mainIdea: Robert Koch proved that specific bacteria cause specific diseases, finding the tuberculosis germ in 1882.
reading: Robert Koch was a German country doctor who turned his home into a lab. He learned to grow bacteria in pure form and to stain them with dyes so they showed up clearly under a microscope. *Bacteria* are one-celled living things; most are harmless, but some cause disease.

In 1882 Koch announced that he had found the bacterium that causes *tuberculosis*, a lung disease that was then one of the leading causes of death in Europe. He announced it on March 24. That date is now World Tuberculosis Day. In 1883 and 1884, working in Egypt and India, his team identified the cholera bacterium, backing up what Snow's maps had shown.

Koch also set out steps to prove a germ causes a disease. Find the germ in every sick person. Grow it pure. Give it to a healthy animal and see the same disease. Find the same germ again. These steps, called Koch's postulates, turned germ theory into careful science.

words.d: one-celled living things; most are harmless or helpful, and some cause disease
a disease caused by bacteria that usually attacks the lungs
Koch's steps for proving that a certain germ causes a certain disease

look.title: Germs Named in the 1800s
look.cite: Dates as given in standard histories of medicine, e.g. Roy Porter, The Greatest Benefit to Mankind, 1997
look.prompt: How many years passed between Snow's 1854 map and the cholera germ being identified? What does that gap show?

check.q: What did Koch find in 1882?
check.why: In 1882 Koch announced the tuberculosis bacterium; March 24 is now World Tuberculosis Day.

check.q: How did Koch's cholera work connect to John Snow?
choices: It found the germ that explained Snow's water evidence
It showed cholera spread by bad air
check.why: Koch's team identified the cholera bacterium, backing up Snow's evidence that water carried the disease.

check.q: Which is one of Koch's postulates?
choices: Grow the germ in pure form
Blame the smell of the air
check.why: Koch's steps included growing the germ pure and showing it causes the same disease in a healthy animal.

lessons.title: Lister and Antiseptics
lessons.mainIdea: In 1867 Joseph Lister used carbolic acid to kill germs in wounds, and far fewer surgery patients died of infection.
reading: Anesthesia made surgery painless, but many patients still died afterward. Their wounds filled with pus and infection. Surgeons wore old coats stiff with blood and did not wash their tools between patients. In Glasgow, Scotland, a surgeon named Joseph Lister read Pasteur's work on microbes and had an idea.

If microbes spoiled broth, perhaps microbes also infected wounds. Lister began using carbolic acid, a chemical already used to treat sewage, to clean wounds, dressings and tools. He tried it on broken bones where the bone had pierced the skin, a kind of injury that often turned deadly.

In 1867 he reported that his patients healed far better. He called his method *antiseptic* surgery. An antiseptic is a chemical that kills germs on skin or wounds. Later surgeons went further with *aseptic* surgery: keeping germs out from the start with sterile gowns, gloves and tools.

words.d: a substance that kills germs on skin, wounds or tools
free of germs; aseptic surgery keeps germs out from the start
completely free of living germs

look.title: Lister's Report
look.text: Lister explained that, since Pasteur had shown that microbes cause decay, wounds could be kept from festering by destroying the germs with a substance such as carbolic acid.
look.cite: Joseph Lister, On the Antiseptic Principle in the Practice of Surgery, The Lancet, 1867
look.prompt: How did Lister use another scientist's discovery to solve a problem in his own field?

check.q: What chemical did Lister use to kill germs in wounds?
check.why: Lister used carbolic acid on wounds, dressings and tools.

check.q: Whose work gave Lister the idea that microbes infected wounds?
check.why: Lister read Pasteur's work showing that microbes cause spoiling and applied it to wounds.

check.q: How is aseptic surgery different from antiseptic surgery?
choices: It keeps germs out from the start with sterile tools and gowns
It kills germs only after surgery ends
check.why: Antiseptic surgery kills germs present; aseptic surgery keeps germs from getting in at all.

lessons.title: How the Big Idea Changed
lessons.mainIdea: Across the 1800s, evidence slowly replaced the miasma idea with germ theory, and that changed daily life.
reading: For centuries, many doctors believed disease came from bad air or from an imbalance of body fluids. These ideas were not silly. Filthy places really did have more disease. But the true cause was usually germs living in the filth, water or food.

The change came piece by piece. Jenner showed that protection could be trained. Semmelweis showed that hands carried danger. Snow showed that water spread cholera. Pasteur showed that microbes came from other microbes. Koch proved which germ caused which disease. Lister showed that killing germs saved lives. No single person did it alone.

Germ theory changed everyday life. Cities built clean water systems and sewers. Hospitals began to scrub and sterilize. Families learned to wash hands, cook food well and keep milk cold. Much of what feels like common sense today began with these tests. Science changed its mind because the evidence was strong.

words.d: facts and observations that show whether an idea is true
an underground pipe that carries waste water away from homes

rows: Snow and the Broad Street pump
look.cite: Dates as given in standard histories of medicine, e.g. Roy Porter, The Greatest Benefit to Mankind, 1997
look.prompt: Which of these steps came before anyone had proved that germs cause disease? What does that tell you about good evidence?

choices: Filthy places really did have more disease

check.why: Jenner, Semmelweis, Snow, Pasteur, Koch and Lister each added evidence over many years.

check.q: Which everyday habit grew out of germ theory?
choices: Washing hands and keeping milk cold
Avoiding bad smells to stay healthy
Carrying flowers to clean the air

check.why: Germ theory led families to wash hands, cook food well and keep milk cold.

review.q: What did John Snow do at the Broad Street pump in 1854?
choices: Convinced leaders to remove the pump handle
Found the cholera germ with a microscope
review.why: Snow's evidence led local leaders to remove the handle of the Broad Street pump.
Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery with carbolic acid in 1867.

review.q: What did Semmelweis and Lister both try to stop?
review.why: Semmelweis used handwashing and Lister used antiseptics, both to stop germs reaching patients.

review.q: Why is Snow called a father of epidemiology?
choices: He found a cause by mapping and counting cases
He grew the first pure bacteria
review.why: Snow tracked who got sick and where, the core method of epidemiology.

review.q: What made Jenner's method work against smallpox?
choices: Cowpox trained the body to resist smallpox
Cowpox killed smallpox germs in the air
review.why: Cowpox was mild but trained the body's defenses to resist smallpox.

review.q: What did the 1846 Boston demonstration show?
review.why: At Massachusetts General Hospital, ether put a patient to sleep so he felt no real pain.

review.q: What did Pasteur's curved-neck flasks show?
choices: Microbes come from other microbes, not from nothing
review.why: The broth stayed clear when microbes were trapped, showing life did not appear on its own.

review.q: How did Koch strengthen germ theory?
choices: He set steps to prove a certain germ causes a certain disease
He mapped cholera deaths in London
He made doctors wash with chlorine
review.why: Koch's postulates gave clear steps to prove that a specific germ causes a specific disease.
